statement.description: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`. You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. You can return the answer in any order.

learning.keyInsight: Instead of looking for a pair that adds to the target, iterate through the array and look for the *complement* (target - current_number) in a hash map.
learning.whyItMatters: This transforms an O(N^2) brute force search into an O(N) lookup. It's the quintessential example of trading space for time, a core concept in software engineering.
learning.lore: Two Sum is famously the first problem on LeetCode and the 'Hello World' of algorithmic interviews. It perfectly demonstrates the power of Hash Maps.

productionFit.title: Fast lookups in relational data
productionFit.explanation: In databases, when joining two tables, instead of a nested loop join (O(N*M)), we can build a hash index on one table to achieve a Hash Join (O(N+M)).

scaleUp.scenario: The array is larger than memory (e.g., Terabytes).
scaleUp.solution: We could use a MapReduce approach or external sorting, but if the data is distributed, we can partition the array across nodes based on the hash of the numbers.

applications: Finding pairs matching specific criteria in distributed logs
hints: A brute force approach would be to check every combination of two numbers. What is the time complexity of that?
If we fix one of the numbers, say 'x', we have to scan the entire array to find the next number 'y' which is value 'target - x'.
Can we change our array into another data structure that gives us a faster look up time for 'y'?

approaches.label: Nested Loops (Brute Force)
approaches.summary: Check every possible pair of elements in the array to see if they sum to the target.
approaches.intuition: Try all combinations. If we are currently at element x, we check all subsequent elements to see if any equal target - x.
algorithm_steps: Iterate j from i + 1 to len(nums).
If nums[i] + nums[j] == target, return [i, j].

time.explanation: For each of the n elements, we loop through the remaining elements.
time.best_case: O(1) if first two elements are the answer

space.explanation: We only use a few variables for iteration.

steps: i=1 (2): check j=2 (4). Sum=6. YES! Return [1, 2]

approaches.label: Two-Pass Hash Map
approaches.summary: Build a hash map of values to indices, then iterate again to find the complement.
approaches.intuition: We can reduce the O(N) inner loop of the brute force to O(1) by using a hash map.
algorithm_steps: Iterate over nums and add each element's value and its index to a hash map.
For each element, calculate complement = target - nums[i].
Check if complement exists in the map and its index is not i.

time.explanation: We traverse the list containing n elements twice.

space.explanation: The extra space required depends on the number of items stored in the hash table.

approaches.label: One-Pass Hash Map (Optimal)
approaches.summary: Check for the complement in the map as you iterate and build it.
approaches.intuition: While we iterate and insert elements into the map, we can look back to see if current element's complement already exists in the map.
algorithm_steps: For each element, calculate complement = target - nums[i].
If complement exists in the map, return [map[complement], i].
Otherwise, add nums[i] to the map with its index i.

time.explanation: We traverse the list containing n elements exactly once. Each lookup in the table costs only O(1) time.

space.explanation: We store at most n elements in the hash map.

steps: i=0, num=2: comp=7. Not in map. add {2: 0}
i=1, num=7: comp=2. YES! in map at index 0. Return [0, 1]

ascii_frames:
[ 2, 7, 11, 15 ]
     ^
     i=1, num=7, map={2:0}
     comp=2 IN map -> return [0, 1]

variations.title: Two Sum II
variations.oneLiner: Input array is sorted; use two pointers instead of a hash map to achieve O(1) space.

variations.title: 3Sum
variations.oneLiner: Find triplets that sum to 0. Usually solved by sorting and using two pointers.

conceptualQuiz.question: Why is the One-Pass Hash Map preferred over the Two-Pass approach?
options: Because it does not require sorting the array.
Because it avoids iterating through the array twice, cutting the execution time in half in the worst case, and avoids matching an element with itself.
Because it handles negative numbers better.
conceptualQuiz.explanation: While both are O(N) time and space, the one-pass avoids a second loop and elegantly prevents the edge case of using the same element twice (because the current element isn't in the map yet when we check for its complement).

debuggingChallenge.bugLocation: The dictionary comprehension overwrites duplicate values with their latest index. Also, it can pair a number with itself if `target = num * 2`.
debuggingChallenge.fix: Use the one-pass approach or explicitly check `hashmap[comp] != i`.
